sources.title: Bongers and colleagues, Indigenous accounting and exchange at Monte Sierpe, Antiquity (2025)
sources.note: Direct full original article read: The Chincha Kingdom; Results; Figures 6 and 8; Discussion; Barter marketplace. Historical specialization derives from later colonial accounts, distinguished from measured pits and plant remains. Barter and storage are interpretations. All sections counted as one work.

sources.title: Lambayeque ecological-economic zoning study, section 79: Museo de Sitio Túcume
sources.note: Official Ministry of Environment repository original PDF indexed text checked, printed page 321. Direct extraction failed. Reproducible query: site.sinia.minam.gob.pe "Túcume" "1375" "1470". Chronology, successive architectural remodeling, 26 adobe pyramids and marine reliefs supported. sources.title: Municipalidad Distrital de Túcume, Historia
sources.note: Direct municipal page read, Historia paragraphs on adobe structures, storerooms, patios, rooms, ramps and kitchens. Mythic Naymlap foundation narrative and superlative irrigation claim are not adopted. Site-wide description does not securely date every kitchen to the mapped interval.

sources.title: Righetti and colleagues, Survey of a Peruvian Archaeological Site Using LiDAR and Photogrammetry (2021)
sources.note: Direct University of Turin institutional abstract read. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-86979-3_43, pages 613 to 628. Abstract verifies 2019 Imperio survey, large walled platform, unsettled political interpretation and planned drainage features. Full chapter restricted and not claimed read.

sources.title: Armando Anzellini, Developing Methods for the Estimation of Stature and Their Use as a Proxy for Health among the Ancient Chachapoya of Peru (2016)
sources.note: Direct University of Central Florida thesis PDF read selectively: abstract and printed pages 25 to 29, especially Kuelap section and Figure 4 (PDF pages 39 to 42). Household structures, agricultural land and varied burial locations verified. Regional political unity remains debated. No stature-to-health simplification or biological-family inference adopted.

sources.title: Kenneth C. Nystrom, Trepanation in the Chachapoya region of northern Perú (2007)
sources.note: Direct author-hosted original journal PDF read: printed pages 40 to 45, Revash sample context, results and Figures 2 to 4. DOI 10.1002/oa.860; publication 2007, online 2006. Revash attributed approximately 1350 to 1470 but old collection lacks precise individual excavation contexts. Healing is supported; indications for most operations remain uncertain. No generalized success percentage adopted.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian, Quipu/Counting record, 14/3866
sources.note: Direct Smithsonian catalog read. Cotton cord and dyes, tied/knotted; place Chulpaca, Ica; catalog date 1450 to 1532; probably Inka, attributed. Collection history unknown before San Marcos University; acquired by exchange in 1925. No numerical or linguistic decoding supplied for this specimen.

sources.title: Manuel Medrano, Knot Just Numbers: Andean Khipu Strings, Gresham College (20 October 2021)
sources.note: Direct scholarly lecture transcript read: Khipus: A brief introduction, paragraphs on cord keepers, chronology, canonical decimal knots and example 2,035. The example is a modern teaching illustration of established numerical conventions, not a transcription of Smithsonian 14/3866. Narrative signs remain incompletely understood.

proposedOverrides.name: Andean states and chiefdoms
proposedOverrides.summary: A regional atlas umbrella for distinct Peruvian communities and powers, including Chincha, Túcume and Kuélap, during centuries of political change.

batchIdentityNotes.identity: Regional historical-basemaps culture umbrella, not one state, ethnos or religious community.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Three essentially repeated Peru polygons. Ray-cast points for Chincha, Kuélap, Túcume and Cusco are inside; Chan Chan, Chancay, Huánuco Pampa and Sillustani are outside. Public overview explicitly cautions that repeated outline cannot represent local frontiers or Inca expansion.
batchIdentityNotes.association: Exact ID only; no aliases. Named Wari and Tiwanaku empires precede much of this interval and are not this umbrella. Existing Chimú, Inca, Aymara, Chanka and Huanca accounts remain separate. Indexed wari is an Amazonian Wari’ people record and must not be mistaken for the ancient Wari Empire.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Public periods remain within 1279 to 1492 and label imported boundaries. Túcume conquest dates are approximate local conventions. Kuélap details span local Late Intermediate and Inca contexts; Revash skull study explicitly dated circa 1350 to 1470 with context limits. Smithsonian specimen broadly dated 1450 to 1532 is a late-period comparison, not securely pre-1492.
batchIdentityNotes.evidenceLimits: No common Andean language, invented inscription, universal school system, family custom, toilet or medicine is claimed. Monte Sierpe exchange/storage are interpretations. Modern numeric illustration is distinguished from the authentic undecoded khipu specimen. No single fall date or unsupported successor link.
